public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Primes and perfect squares

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau%27s_problems#Near-square_primes)
-/

@[expose] public section


namespace PrimesAndPerfectSquares

/--
Are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p - 1$ is a perfect square? In other words: Are there infinitely many primes of the form $n^2 + 1$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem infinite_prime_sq_add_one :
    answer(sorry) ↔ {n : ℕ | Prime (n^2 + 1)}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end PrimesAndPerfectSquares

reformulations.difference: The source asks whether there are infinitely many primes p with p − 1 a perfect square, i.e. primes of the form n² + 1 for integer n. The Lean statement instead says that the set of natural numbers n with `Prime (n^2 + 1)` is infinite: it counts the parameters n rather than the primes, and n ranges over ℕ rather than ℤ. It also uses `_root_.Prime` on ℕ rather than `Nat.Prime`.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The map n ↦ n² + 1 is injective on ℕ, so the Lean set is infinite exactly when its image is. That image is exactly the set of primes p with p − 1 a square: p ≥ 2, so the truncated subtraction p − 1 behaves normally, and p − 1 = r·r gives p = r² + 1. The image is also the set of primes p = n² + 1 with n ∈ ℤ, because n² = |n|² for every integer. `_root_.Prime p ↔ Nat.Prime p` on ℕ by `Nat.prime_iff`. Both equivalences, `{n : ℕ | Prime (n^2 + 1)}.Infinite ↔ {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ IsSquare (p - 1)}.Infinite` and `{n : ℕ | Prime (n^2 + 1)}.Infinite ↔ {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ ∃ n : ℤ, (p : ℤ) = n^2 + 1}.Infinite`, were proved in the scratch file using `Set.infinite_image_iff`. The answer slot has the source's polarity: an infinite set is the 'yes' answer.

sources_consulted: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau%27s_problems (raw wikitext via https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Landau%27s_problems&action=raw), including the intro list and the 'Near-square primes' section
review.notes: The file has one declaration, and it states Landau's fourth problem faithfully. The docstring repeats Wikipedia's wording word for word. The Lean statement is `answer(sorry) ↔ {n : ℕ | Prime (n^2 + 1)}.Infinite`, which has the right polarity: `answer(True)` is the positive answer. It elaborates to `True ↔ …` because of the repository-wide `alwaysTrue` default of the `answer` elaborator; nothing about this is specific to the file. Checks: `Prime` resolves to `_root_.Prime` on ℕ with `Nat.instCommMonoidWithZero`, which is equivalent to `Nat.Prime`. `#eval` of the predicate on n < 60 gives [1, 2, 4, 6, 10, 14, 16, 20, 24, 26, 36, 40, 54, 56], the expected values. n = 0 is correctly excluded, since 1 is not prime. Equivalence with both source phrasings (p − 1 a perfect square; n² + 1 with n an integer) was proved in Lean. Status: Wikipedia says 'As of 2026, all four problems are unresolved', which matches `research open`. I could not read the OEIS pages A005574 and A002496 (Cloudflare challenge), but they are not needed.
